expansion:
A. Geographic corneal ulcer is the keyed answer. The steroid exposure followed by worsening painful photophobic red eye and a large epithelial ulcer fits steroid-exacerbated epithelial herpes simplex keratitis presenting as a geographic ulcer. The lecture describes epithelial HSV as “Dendritic / Geographic,” states that “Geographic = large irregular lesion,” and warns: “NEVER use topical steroids in EPITHELIAL herpes keratitis” because they promote viral replication and can result in perforation (L15,16, page 13; L15,16, page 15). It further specifically states that topical steroids in epithelial HSV “Can cause geographic ulcer” (L15,16, page 48). The terms “amoeboid” and “scalloped borders” are not stated in the course material; the course instead describes the geographic lesion as “large irregular” (L15,16, page 14).

B. Acanthamoeba keratitis is wrong because its taught pattern is contact lens wear with tap-water or swimming exposure, severe pain out of proportion, early perineural infiltrates, and a late ring infiltrate (L15,16, page 17). These discriminating features are not given, whereas the steroid-associated geographic epithelial ulcer is explicitly taught for HSV.

C. Bacterial corneal ulcer is wrong because the lecture associates it with rapid onset, mucopurulent discharge, a large central/paracentral ulcer, hypopyon, and contact lens history (L15,16, page 19). A geographic ulcer after inappropriate topical steroid treatment instead points to epithelial HSV.

D. Fungal keratitis is wrong because the course associates it with trauma from plant matter, feathery satellite lesions, slower onset, and Sabouraud culture; topical steroid history can occur but is not the defining morphology here (L15,16, page 19).
objective: Recognize that topical corticosteroids can exacerbate epithelial HSV keratitis and produce a geographic corneal ulcer.
